title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
summary: The depth of a tree is 1 (for the root) plus the deeper of its two subtrees. An empty tree has depth 0. Recursion computes it bottom-up: each node waits for its children's depths.

complexity.note: Every node is visited once; the call stack is as deep as the tree (h), O(n) for a skewed tree.

intuition: Base case: `null` has depth 0.
Recursive case: `1 + max(depth(left), depth(right))`.
BFS counting levels gives the same answer iteratively.
pitfalls: Returning 1 for a null node (off by one).
Very deep skewed trees can overflow the call stack; BFS avoids recursion.

title: Invert Binary Tree
summary: Mirror a tree: swap every node's left and right children. Swap at the current node, then invert both subtrees (or the other way round); every node gets swapped exactly once.

complexity.note: One swap per node; recursion depth h.

intuition: Mirroring a tree = swap the children, then mirror each child.
Pre-order and post-order both work; in-order does not (it re-swaps one side).
Return the root so the call can be chained.

Python.code:
def invertTree(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> Optional[TreeNode]:
    if not root: return None
    root.left, root.right = root.right, root.left
    invertTree(root.left)
    invertTree(root.right)
    return root

title: Same Tree
summary: Two trees are the same when they have the same shape and values. Walk both at once: two nulls match, one null doesn't, and otherwise the values must match and both pairs of subtrees must be the same.
intuition: Compare structure and value at each pair of nodes.
Both null → true; exactly one null → false.
`&&` short-circuits, so a mismatch on the left skips the right side.
pitfalls: Comparing only in-order traversals: different shapes can give the same sequence.
Checking `p.val == q.val` before checking for null.

title: Balanced Binary Tree
summary: A tree is height-balanced when, at every node, the two subtree heights differ by at most 1. Compute heights bottom-up and return -1 as soon as any subtree is unbalanced, so the whole check is one pass.

complexity.note: Each node's height is computed once.

intuition: Checking balance top-down with a separate height function is O(n²) on skewed trees.
Return height when balanced and -1 when not, in a single recursion.
Once a child reports -1, pass -1 straight up.
pitfalls: Only checking the root's two subtrees; every node must be balanced.
Confusing balanced with complete or full.

title: Diameter of Binary Tree
category: Trees · Height with a global best
summary: The diameter is the longest path (in edges) between any two nodes. The longest path through a node is `height(left) + height(right)`. Compute heights bottom-up and keep the best sum seen.
intuition: Every path has a highest node; at that node it's left height + right height.
The recursion returns height; the diameter is tracked on the side.
The path doesn't have to pass through the root.
pitfalls: Assuming the diameter goes through the root.

Python.code:
def diameterOfBinaryTree(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
    best = 0

    def depth(node: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
        nonlocal best
        if not node: return 0
        left = depth(node.left)
        right = depth(node.right)
        best = max(best, left + right)
        return 1 + max(left, right)

    depth(root)
    return best

title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
summary: Return node values level by level, left to right. Use a queue: at the start of each round, the queue holds exactly one level. Pop that many nodes, record their values, and push their children for the next level.

complexity.note: w = the widest level, up to n/2.

intuition: A queue processes nodes in the order they were discovered: breadth-first.
Snapshot `size = queue.size()` to know where the current level ends.
Children are added left before right.
pitfalls: Forgetting the size snapshot mixes levels together.
Adding null children to the queue.

title: Binary Tree Right Side View
summary: Standing on the right, you see the last node of each level. Do a level-order traversal and record the value of the last node popped in every level.
intuition: The rightmost node of a level is the last one popped in that round.
Left children still matter: a left node is visible if the right side is shorter.
A DFS visiting right first and recording the first node at each depth also works.
pitfalls: Only following right children misses deeper left nodes.
Recording the first node of each level instead of the last.

title: Binary Tree Zigzag Level Order Traversal
summary: Like level order, but alternate direction each level: left-to-right, then right-to-left. Do a normal BFS and, on odd levels, insert values at the front of the level's list instead of the back.

complexity.note: Adding to the front of a LinkedList is O(1).

intuition: The traversal order never changes; only where values go in the level list.
Flip a boolean after each level.
`LinkedList.addFirst` reverses a level without a separate reverse step.
pitfalls: Changing the order children are queued breaks later levels.
Reversing with `Collections.reverse` is fine but an extra pass.
